mercy_translation.text:
Accordingly, the Word of God assumed a body and used a human instrument, so that he might give life to the body and, just as he is known in creation through his works, so he might also work in a human being and show himself everywhere, leaving nothing empty of his divinity and of the knowledge of himself.

I repeat what I said before: the Savior did this so that, just as by his presence he fills all things everywhere, so he might also fill all things with the knowledge of himself, as divine Scripture says: “The whole earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord.”

If someone wishes to look up to heaven, he sees its ordering. If he cannot look to heaven but looks only to human beings, he sees through the works Christ's incomparable power among human beings and knows that he alone among them is God the Word. If someone has turned toward demons and is fascinated by them, he sees Christ driving them away and judges him to be their Master. If someone has sunk into the nature of waters and thinks water is God—as the Egyptians worship water—he sees water changed by Christ and learns that the Lord is its Creator.

If someone descends even into Hades and is fascinated by the heroes who went down there as though they were gods, he sees Christ's resurrection and his victory over death and concludes that among them Christ alone is true Lord and God.

For the Lord touched every part of creation and freed and exposed all things from every deception, as Paul says: “Having stripped the principalities and powers, he triumphed over them in the cross,” so that no one might any longer be deceived but everywhere find the true Word of God.

Thus human beings are, as it were, enclosed from every side and see the divinity of the Word spread everywhere—in heaven, in Hades, in humanity, and on earth. They are no longer deceived concerning God, but worship him alone and through him rightly know the Father.

By these reasonable arguments the Greeks may therefore be put to shame. But if they do not consider the arguments sufficient, let them at least be convinced by the things manifest before everyone's eyes.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius presents Christ's work as touching every sphere in which humanity had sought divinity or spiritual power.
The chapter prepares the move from philosophical argument to empirical/apologetic claims about Christian expansion.
